Teaching labs for measurement courses

Source: vignettes/articles/teaching-labs.Rmd
teaching-labs.Rmd

mirtverse ships interactive labs for university measurement courses. They are learnr tutorials: students read a short brief, run real R code against live mirt models, and answer decision questions that explain why each choice holds up or doesn’t. The goal is not only to learn the mirt syntax but to practise the judgment calls of a working analyst. For a short introduction to share with students, see Learn IRT by doing.

install.packages("learnr")   # once
library(mirtverse)
list_labs()
run_lab("model-choice")   # Lab 1
run_lab("decisions")      # Lab 2

The labs also appear in RStudio’s Tutorial pane once mirtverse and learnr are installed. Students’ progress is saved on their computer, so they can stop and pick up where they left off.

The storyline

Both labs follow one scenario. Students are the new psychometrician for the fictional Northfield Certification Board. The board’s 32-item, five-option exam was taken by 1,200 candidates in English or French, and the board wants to move from number-correct to IRT scoring.

The data, certexam, are simulated from item parameters based on a 3PL calibration of mirt’s SAT12 data, so the items behave like real ones. Because the data were generated, the truth is known, and a few problems were planted on purpose:

Planted problem Where students meet it What a good analyst does
Q14 is miskeyed in certexam_key Lab 1, item screening Spots the negative item-total correlation, checks the key with a distractor analysis, fixes it and rescores
Q21 and Q22 share a reading passage Lab 1, dimensionality and local dependence Recognises a two-item “factor” as local dependence, not a second trait; treats the pair as a testlet
Guessing on harder items (the true model is the 3PL) Lab 1, model comparison Weighs AIC against BIC, convergence and sample size; 2PL and 3PL are both defensible, Rasch is not
Q09 (uniform) and Q27 (non-uniform) show DIF against French candidates Lab 2, fairness Flags both for content review
French candidates score 0.35 SD lower on average Lab 2, fairness Separates a real group difference (impact) from DIF

lab_truth() returns the generating values for instructors.

Lab 1: Choosing a model the board can defend

run_lab("model-choice"), about 75 minutes.

Section Students do Decision
The brief Meet the board and the raw data
Score the responses key2binary() Why score before fitting?
Screen the items Proportion correct and corrected item-total correlations, a distractor analysis, fix the key What to do with a negative item-total correlation; which option is the real key
How many dimensions? One- vs two-factor 2PL, anova(), rotated loadings Is one dimension defensible?
Compare the models select_model() on Rasch, 2PL, 3PL Which model to recommend
Check the chosen model gg_itemfit(), gg_q3() How to treat flagged item fit; what to do about Q21 and Q22
Commit to a model Fit final, write a justification Free-text justification, then a model answer
Your decisions A table of every answer the student gave

Every decision question explains why each option holds up or doesn’t, so a wrong answer becomes a teaching moment:

At the end, students see every choice they made:

Answer key

  • Why score first: the 2PL and 3PL model the probability of a correct answer.
  • Negative item-total correlation: check the key before anything else.
  • Real key for Q14: A. About 90% of the top 20% of candidates chose it; the published key says C.
  • Dimensions: one. The likelihood-ratio test and AIC favour two factors, BIC favours one, and the second factor is made only of Q21 and Q22.
  • Model: the 2PL (lowest BIC, converges, M2 RMSEA about 0.015) or the 3PL (lowest AIC, but it does not converge with default settings and its guessing parameters are poorly determined at N = 1,200). Both are accepted; the feedback names the trade-off. Rasch is rejected by every criterion.
  • Item fit: a couple of items have p < .01, but after a false-discovery-rate correction none is flagged at that level, and the misfit is small (RMSEA about 0.03).
  • Q21 and Q22: Q3 of about 0.27, more than twice any other pair. Combine them into a testlet score, model the passage, or keep one item; at minimum, report it.

Discussion prompts

  • The likelihood-ratio test rejected one dimension. Why is that not enough to conclude the exam measures two traits?
  • The true model is the 3PL, yet BIC prefers the 2PL. Is BIC “wrong”? What is model selection trying to find?
  • A candidate who failed by one point appeals. Which parts of your analysis would you want to show the appeal panel?

Lab 2: From parameters to decisions

run_lab("decisions"), about 75 minutes. The board’s 2PL model is fitted in the lab’s setup, so students can start Lab 2 without finishing Lab 1.

Section Students do Decision
Read the items coef(IRTpars = TRUE), gg_trace() Which item is hardest and what its low slope means; reading a trace line
Precision at the pass mark Map the raw cut of 18 to theta with the EAP sum-score table; gg_info(), testinfo() Is the exam precise enough at the cut, and what items would help?
Choose a scoring method Compare EAP, ML and sum-score scale scores What goes on candidates’ score reports
Classification accuracy Misclassification probabilities from each candidate’s score and SE How to respond to measurement error near the cut
Fairness across languages Raw means by group, dif(), gg_dif() Impact versus DIF; what to do with the flagged items
The memo Free-text memo, then interpret() and item_card()
The reveal lab_truth(), true versus estimated difficulties Where the 2PL departs from the true 3PL

Answer key

  • Hardest item: Q32 (b about 3), with Q12 close behind. Both have low slopes (about 0.45), the 2PL’s way of absorbing guessing.
  • Trace line: at theta = 0, Q32’s probability is about 0.2.
  • Pass mark: raw 18 corresponds to theta of about 0.05. Information there is about 6 (SE about 0.41), close to the exam’s peak at theta of about -0.5. Medium-difficulty, highly discriminating items would help most.
  • Scoring: scale scores from the sum-score table (every candidate with the same raw score gets the same score) are the most defensible for certification; pattern EAP is accepted with the caveat about explaining it. ML is undefined for perfect and zero scores.
  • Classification: about 145 of 1,200 candidates (12%) are expected to be misclassified, and about 364 (30%) are within one SE of the cut. Report it, and consider a retest policy or more items near the cut; don’t move the cut.
  • Impact: French candidates are estimated 0.38 SD lower (true value 0.35). That is a group difference, not item bias.
  • DIF: only Q09 (uniform; about 15 percentage points harder for French candidates at the same ability) and Q27 (non-uniform; the curves cross) are flagged. Send both to bilingual content review.
  • Truth: the 2PL departs most from the true difficulties for the hardest items, where guessing matters.

Discussion prompts

  • Two candidates both answered 18 items correctly. Under pattern scoring one passes and one fails. How would you explain that to them? Would you?
  • Q27’s average (signed) DIF effect is small. Why is that misleading?
  • The board’s 2PL was “wrong”, yet most of the decisions it supported were right. When does using a simpler model than the truth matter?

Tips for instructors

  • Before class: ask students to install mirtverse and learnr and run list_labs(). Fitting the models needs no internet connection.
  • Speed: every exercise runs in under about 15 seconds on a laptop; the two-factor model uses fewer quadrature points so it stays quick.
  • Hosting: to run a lab in the browser without any installation, deploy the tutorial folder (system.file("tutorials", "model-choice", package = "mirtverse")) to shinyapps.io or Posit Connect. learnr’s event recorder (options(tutorial.event_recorder = ...)) can log students’ answers there.
  • Assessment: the free-text justification at the end of each lab makes a good short assignment. Ask students to paste it, together with their decision table, into your course site.
